name: Valeriy and Deque
description: Recently, on the course of algorithms and data structures, Valeriy learned how to use a deque. He built a deque filled with $$$n$$$ elements. The $$$i$$$-th element is $$$a_i$$$ ($$$i$$$ = $$$1, 2, \ldots, n$$$). He gradually takes the first two leftmost elements from the deque (let's call them $$$A$$$ and $$$B$$$, respectively), and then does the following: if $$$A \gt B$$$, he writes $$$A$$$ to the beginning and writes $$$B$$$ to the end of the deque, otherwise, he writes to the beginning $$$B$$$, and $$$A$$$ writes to the end of the deque. We call this sequence of actions an operation. For example, if deque was $$$[2, 3, 4, 5, 1]$$$, on the operation he will write $$$B=3$$$ to the beginning and $$$A=2$$$ to the end, so he will get $$$[3, 4, 5, 1, 2]$$$. The teacher of the course, seeing Valeriy, who was passionate about his work, approached him and gave him $$$q$$$ queries. Each query consists of the singular number $$$m_j$$$ $$$(j = 1, 2, \ldots, q)$$$. It is required for each query to answer which two elements he will pull out on the $$$m_j$$$-th operation. Note that the queries are independent and for each query the numbers $$$A$$$ and $$$B$$$ should be printed in the order in which they will be pulled out of the deque . Deque is a data structure representing a list of elements where insertion of new elements or deletion of existing elements can be made from both sides.
input_specification: The first line contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$q$$$ ($$$2 \leq n \leq 10^5$$$, $$$0 \leq q \leq 3 \cdot 10^5$$$) — the number of elements in the deque and the number of queries. The second line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_1$$$, $$$a_2$$$, ..., $$$a_n$$$, where $$$a_i$$$ $$$(0 \leq a_i \leq 10^9)$$$ — the deque element in $$$i$$$-th position. The next $$$q$$$ lines contain one number each, meaning $$$m_j$$$ ($$$1 \leq m_j \leq 10^{18}$$$).
output_specification: For each teacher's query, output two numbers $$$A$$$ and $$$B$$$ — the numbers that Valeriy pulls out of the deque for the $$$m_j$$$-th operation.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1179A — Valeriy and Deque [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
